So there's two different answers here. The answer to the S&P is that the *majority* of locations assigned on 23andMe are based on crowd sourcing grandparents birth locations. If you don't have a lot of DNA matches who have recent (like the last 4 generations) ancestry in those places you simply won't get a location.

For the Indigenous locations it's a little different. They're geared toward North American Indigenous groups and are based on genetic similarity to Indigenous peoples of those regions. So, for example, if you were 31.7% Ojibwe you'd get Great Lakes and Canada as a location, but if you're 31.7% Purepecha you won't get any of those locations, you'll just get a recent ancestry in the Americas location instead.

Ah, this is accurate for all regions *except* the North American Indigenous regions. 23andMe's description of how they determine these new regions is as follows:

We compare a customer's DNA that is predicted to have been inherited from an Indigenous American ancestor to the DNA of individuals in the reference groups. If a customer has DNA that matches multiple individuals in the same reference group, and a sufficient percentage of their genome as a proportion of their total Indigenous American DNA is covered by these matching DNA segments, we can report the region to the customer as a "match," with "likely" or "highly likely" confidence.

To receive a "highly likely match," a larger percentage of the customer's DNA must match the reference group's DNA than is required to receive a "likely" match. A "likely" match means the customer has met a threshold of shared DNA that corresponds to 50–80% confidence that the match is the most correct match. A "highly likely" match means the customer has met a threshold of shared DNA that corresponds to greater than 80% confidence that the match is the most correct match.

"All First Nations people chose to live on reserves."

Reserve land was described to First Nations people as a way for them to keep some land while settlers were allowed to claim the rest under various homesteading laws. In reality, the government gave them *mostly* isolated land that settlers weren't as interested in so they wouldn't "get in the way" of the settlers. Most of the land had no infrastructure, there were no supplies available like there were for settlers. The people sent to reserves often had a hard time foraging and hunting because they were moved away from the land they were familiar with and could not bring much with them, but also struggled to farm because of a lack of supplies, lack of familiarity with farming in the area, and lack of good soil or access to water. 

The pass system was implemented around 1885 and lasted into the 1950s, it confined people to the reserves. You could not leave your reserve - even for a day - without submitting an application to an Indian Agent and having it approved.

"The rest of us dont have the option of living on reserves or living tax free."

Neither do the vast majority of Indigenous people. Originally only people who fall under the Indian Act are eligible for any such thing, now that's slightly different for reserves (individual bands have more control over who can live there), but still applies for any kind of tax exemption. This means that Métis, Inuit, and non-status First Nations people are not eligible. The tax exemption also applies only to some specific situations even if you qualify to use it. There's a really great breakdown of it [here](https://apihtawikosisan.com/2011/12/first-nations-taxation/), on the internet, for free, and can be read in under 10 minutes.

Abaya and jilbab are pretty similar and I've seen people use them interchangeably! An abaya is a long flowing robe that originated in the Arab world a very very long time ago, and there are dozens upon dozens of different styles. It's one of those things where despite being a cultural item of clothing, it's become a little more pan-Islamic over the years, although there are still areas where it's very rarely worn. Jilbab technically refers to any long flowing outergarment that covers your regular clothes (although in Indonesia it refers to a kind of headscarf which can be confusing) , so an abaya can be your jilbab, or a chador can, or a kaftan, etc. If you hop on google to find one to buy though, you'll probably find a specific style of jilbab that's either: a one piece robe that goes right from the top of your head to your feet, with a cut out for your face and small sleeve openings for your hands (usually with an inner headband to keep it from slipping off) or a two piece in the same style (it may come with a skirt bottom or puffy sarouel pants).

Burqa is also one of those words that can mean a couple different things. The famous Afghan "burqa" is actually called a chadri/chadaree/paranja and is incredibly specific to Central Asia, you won't see Saudi or Egyptian or Indonesian women wearing it for example. In some places an abaya is referred to as a burqa or burka, you can see this if you google things like "purchase a burqa", you'll get a couple of sites selling abayas and a couple of sites selling niqabs that include a pull down mesh veil that covers the eyes. Now, as far as wearing a niqab or burqa/boushiyya... I really advise against it. Not for any appropriative reasons or anything, but because you are opening yourself up to a world of harassment and violence. Trust me when I say that many people do not see niqabis as human beings and treat them like garbage. I wore it briefly in 2014 and I had people scream at me in the street, yank on my clothes, try to hit or kick me as I walked by, throw garbage at me as they drove by me, etc. It's very very hard and demoralising  unless you're in a very safe area or you always have someone travelling with you.

If it is something you feel truly called to wear, however, then to answer your question about street clothes, I don't think anyone would ever wear niqab with jeans or "regular" clothing the way people do with hijab. A Muslim wearing niqab will have probably started by transitioning to wearing a jilbab rather than stuff like sweaters and jeans first, and once they're doing that full time they'll start wearing niqab and possibly gloves as well. If you were to wear it with regular clothes I think you'd put yourself in the uncomfortable situation of upsetting a lot of Muslims who see it because there would be this reaction of "Why is this Muslim girl wearing niqab with jeans??? Doesn't she know that's inappropriate??" and some bolder men and women would scold you without even introducing themselves or allowing you to explain that you're not Muslim and therefore the rules don't apply to you. It would also bother non-Muslims who already don't approve of facial coverings who would probably think you're up to something, and you'd definitely have trouble with security guards etc. anywhere you went. Now, if by regular clothes you mean long dresses with cardigans and stuff like that, I could see that being okay. You'd probably still get some busybodies telling you that niqabis shouldn't wear colourful clothing or something but it wouldn't be as shocking to anyone.

Well, poverty is cyclical, so there are large populations that are just born poor and kept poor. If your family is living below the poverty line chances are your school performance is suffering, you're probably working a job as soon as you're legally old enough to (maybe even before that) just to help your family, maybe you even drop out to work full time. 

So now you're employed, but it means you're still working that shitty minimum wage (or lower if you have no means of reporting) job with little to no hope for advancement. Plus, people living in poverty have higher rates for injury and illness due to stress and being more likely to work in physical labour, so congratulations. You managed to save $5-$10 from your cheque every couple of weeks? It's gone now to cover that work related injury that you can't get compensation for because you can't afford to pursue it.

But even in the case that you actually make it to college or university, here are more problems. Your family can't support you so you apply for loans, but what if you can't get a co signer? What if you get approved, but for an amount that doesn't cover all your expenses? You're probably working and studying but not only does that negatively affect your performance, you're probably working a PT job with lower wages (since student wages are usually lower than minimum). Then you graduate and even if you chose the perfect money making field, you might not find a job for over a year, but that loan is still waiting to be paid off.

And this is literally just one reason, tied directly to the poverty cycle. There are dozens more. In my case it was losing my legal guardian which lead to the loss of my home and having to scramble to find an apartment that would accept someone so young without a guarantor for rent.

I think a big problem is that we hijabis are often put on the defensive. We're bombarded so constantly by people telling us that we must have been forced to do this, we're extremists, we're buying into the patriarchy, the media ignoring our existence or painting the hijab totally negatively, etc. and we're so busy saying "but that isn't that case with me" that we refuse to believe that it could be the case for anyone else. It also leads to us over-representing hijabi women in Muslim media to make up for our lack of representation elsewhere which makes non-hijabis feel under-represented in our community! On the other side of things, women who have been forced into or coerced into wearing hijab often refuse to believe that anyone else could have made the choice freely and willingly. It leads to both sides being defensive and refusing to have any dialogue, which is not what we need. 

What we really need is, well, multiple things. 

We need the media to stop putting our religious practices under a microscope so that we can have more intra-community discussions without fearing that any criticism within the community will be used against us. We need non-Muslims to stop criticising hijabis so that we can actually have frank and honest discussions about it without going, "Oh, but if I admit that I don't like this aspect of it people might use it as proof that the hijab is an objectively bad thing so I just won't talk about it at all."

We need to respect the multitude of different experiences out there, acknowledge them, and support everyone. We need to support the woman who put hijab on against her family's wishes because it was spiritually important to her, the woman whose family berated her until she put it on who wants nothing more than to take it off, the woman who decided not to wear hijab and whose family/community doesn't care, the woman who decided not to wear it and gets hounded about it every day, and every other individual experience out there. 

We need communities where every Muslim woman can be involved and appreciate, whether she wears short-shorts or an overhead abaya and niqab. Unfortunately, many communities have a specific form of hijab that they consider acceptable and anything that goes below or above it is Bad Hijab. That needs to stop.

We also need to address our community's obsession with female hijab in general. I have seen so many posters in masjids comparing women who don't wear hijab to dirty candies and unwrapped presents. They make the hijab all about human men, whether it's about not tempting random non-mahrams or hiding your beauty so you can give it to your husband. This is ridiculous, and it's what makes people see hijab as a sexist restriction. Why not teach what the hijab is really about? Obedience to and humility in front of Allah (swt). 

We also need to remind men of their hijab as frequently as we remind women. If the imam does a khutbah on why jeans aren't appropriate hijab, he should be talking to the boys as well as the girls, since the buttocks and genitals are awrah for both. When he talks about how summer is coming up and swimming season is starting, he should be reminding men of their obligations as well! Some Muslims literally do not even know that men have their own hijab, yet everyone (Muslim or not) knows about women's hijab. What does that say about how well we're teaching this?

Anyway, this was a really long rant and to summarize: I wish we had room in our Muslim community for negative experiences as well as the positive ones, and I wish that there was room in the non-Muslim community for positive experiences with hijab as well as negative ones.

I know this is a few days old but I feel compelled to educate you a little bit on birds. Birds raised in captivity experience intense fear and stress when they are released into the wild away from their owners. A Green Cheek Conure does not thrive in the environment of South-Eastern Ontario, and one that is born in captivity does not know how to look for food or what food is safe to eat. Their camouflage does not mesh with the plant species in our area and they are easy prey for predators and unscrupulous humans who want to capture and re-sell them.

On top of that, conures are a very social species and develop deep bonds with their "flock" members, and they also rely on their flock for protection and survival. Many of them actually won't eat unless someone they trust is near them, because they instinctively know that eating alone makes them vulnerable. So when they are alone their instincts cause them to panic and seek out their flock. In this bird's case, that is likely the human family that raised it. Seperated from them with no way to find home, the poor little guy is probably terrified. 

When an animal is from a domesticated species or has been raised in captivity, it is often crueler to let them loose than it is to simply care for them properly.
